newsitem.title: UK: UK consumer credit still seen robust despite dip.
newsitem.headline: UK consumer credit still seen robust despite dip.

text.p: A surprise dip in the growth of UK consumer credit in October does little to change expectations of higher interest rates as the underlying trend in the demand for credit remains robust, economists said on Friday.

"The underlying trend for consumer demand remains pretty buoyant," said James Barty, economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. Other recent data clearly shows consumer demand is growing very strongly, he added. Net consumer credit rose by a seasonally-adjusted 856 million stg compared with 1.041 billion stg in September.

Economists said while consumer credit figures can be erratic from month to month, consumer demand overall was still looking very strong. Philip Uglow, economist at Union Discount, said the data did not dent the argument for another rate rise.

"The figures were weaker than we expected, but I don't think they add anything new to the interest rate debate. Recent credit figures and even this morning's show that consumer demand is bubbling along at quite a healthy pace," he said.
Bank of England Governor Eddie George and Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke are due to have their next monetary meeting on December 11.
Clarke agreed to a quarter point rate rise on October 30, taking base rates to 6.0 percent, but he is expected to come under pressure from George next month to raise them again.

Most economic data suggest the recovery is speeding up and recent inflation data has been disappointingly strong. Analysts said the small dip in the growth of consumer credit will not be enough to challenge arguments for higher rates.

"The Chancellor may try to use the softer-than-anticipated overall figure, but the bottom line is that the consumer sector recovery is gathering pace and it is just a matter of time before rates go up again," said Jeremy Hawkins, senior economic adviser at BankAmerica.
A pick up in the housing market in recent months has also helped feed consumer confidence. Higher mortgage borrowing is now feeding through to overall lending data.
"The mortgage lending figures look a bit more important in October and they were very strong. In part this might reflect a last minute dash for mortgages before rates go up," Uglow said.

Despite the base rate rise, most major mortgage lenders kept home loan rates steady. The Halifax Building Society said earlier this week it would wait until the next monetary meeting before taking a decision on its mortgage rates.
Lending secured on dwellings rose by 1.775 billion stg in October compared with 1.399 in September. The three-month growth rate edged up to 4.9 percent from 4.5 in September.
The government welcomed the data and a Treasury official said it showed increasing activity in the housing market and continuing strong consumer demand.
Final M4 money supply figures for October also released on Friday showed broad money accelerated by an unrevised 10.3 percent in the year to October.
